utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, we thought that yesterday we had heard all the submissions on the question of Mr. Coo's evidence, and I've just been handed what's called Sreten Lukic's additional submission objecting to the introduction of Coo documents from the bar table." Now, what does this relate to?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this relates to basically memorialising objections that we would make orally with respect to exhibits that are now being tendered through Mr. Coo. The final list was received at 7.00 in the evening of the exhibits that were still in play with respect to Mr. Coo upon reviewing the submission by Mr. Ackerman on behalf of General Pavkovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How do these differ, though, from the situation we were in yesterday where we had submissions on behalf of the accused Pavkovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: These are not on that list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- on behalf of Sainovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: These are not on that list, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: These objections are not objections that are on that list. These --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but why didn't you object at the same time as everyone else?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we were in the midst of doing everything else --.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- and we couldn't be certain that the -- that there would be 400 exhibits that everything was covered. Now with the 100 -- or excuse me -- 200-or-so-odd exhibits, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ivetic, the Trial Chamber has spent hours, I assure you, on this, hours --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- at various stages and we thought that yesterday when we were spending a great deal of time on it, we had everybody's submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it wasn't until 6.30 in the evening that the Trial Chamber advised us of it's decision that it was going to be treating the Coo submission as a motion for admission of evidence and that all responses would be treated as responses, so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that didn't change the situation at all. These are things we would have expected you to see, whether Coo was -- or whether his report was going to be in evidence or whether it was going to be regarded as a motion for the admission of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we made the general objections when we made our oral objections previously. These are just specifically tying them to specific exhibits within -- so that we don't have to keep objecting every two minutes during the direct examination they want to introduce documents into evidence, so they're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have prepared myself for this morning. I've identified the documents to which objection was taken, and I take it that these are additional to the ones that have been objected in the submissions by Messrs. Pavkovic and Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: They are not on that list; however, at least one -- I think at least one of the documents was discussed yesterday and Your Honours brought it to the attention of the Prosecution, so you may have some of these documents already on your list depending on how it was prepared. I know that there is one document that was the one that unsigned, blank, not yet completed, a draft for some sort of an ambush plan that we did discuss yesterday, which I don't know how it came into discussion since I don't find it on the objections that were filed by the other defendants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And this is confined, is it, to the latest list of exhibits that the Prosecution seek to actually tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic -- sorry. Mr. Fila, I wonder if you can assist with one matter. In paragraph 9 of the submission which you made, while the submission challenges a large number of media reports, it identifies two in particular, one relating to the documentary which included the interview of Goran Radosavljevic and the other was an interview of Blagoje Grahovac. Are both of these now removed from the Prosecution's list, as far as you can see?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are no longer there, and I would like to thank Mr. Hannis because this is now a moot subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, a number of items have been produced as the result of requests for assistance. It would appear that some of the material is simply presented without either the request or the response being submitted. Now, that may be okay. I just want to be clear that you've taken account of the possibility that in some instances the position can only be fully explained as if either the RFA or its response is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I had intended to ask Mr. Coo about that live as to the nature of the response -- of the request for assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you have some other comment to make, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I wanted to address a few remarks before we had the witness come in, and in light of the e-mail last night I wanted to make sure my understanding was correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to deliver a decision at this stage --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- and if you want to await that, you can then seek clarification if something is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, I'll wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is a Norwegian or Norse expression which comes fairly close to describing the events surrounding the process of getting to the point of hearing Mr. Coo give evidence, and that is a saga. I need not go into the detail of that at this stage, save to indicate, as I've already done in part, that a very considerable effort has been put in by the Trial Chamber and support staff to try to make the production of material by Mr. Coo a meaningful exercise and not simply an exercise of tendering everything and anything that might have the remotest bearing on the trial and leaving it to be sorted out later. Parties should know clearly that what they may have to answer is material which has a genuine bearing on the issues in this trial. Having considered the report yet again, we have decided that it should not be admitted as part of Mr. Coo's evidence. The interests of justice militate against that, and therefore by applying Rules 92 ter and 89(F) we refuse to allow that process to supplement his evidence. And that's largely because it still contains expressions of opinion that he is not qualified to give, either because they are matters for the Court or for an expert. It would be impractical to try to fillet the report by deleting these items and -- at this stage in the proceedings. In any event, the comments he can make, generally speaking, add little to the documents themselves now. The Prosecution's principal concern at this stage is to secure the admission of a large number of documents about which Coo appears able to confirm the source and authenticity, relevance and probative value. And by using these expressions, I mean their prima facie authenticity, relevance, and probative value. Until I received Mr. Lukic's submission, I thought only a limited number of these had been put in issue by the Defence. It now appears that a larger number than we anticipated are put in issue. The Trial Chamber already has written submissions from both sides on all the documents. The report should be filed as part of the motion -- or as the motion for admission of the documents, as suggested yesterday by Mr. Ackerman. Now, that requires no alteration of the document except its status, and it's a purely administrative exercise. It will not form part of the record of proceedings as we consider them ultimately at the stage of 98 bis or final judgement. The effect of our decision today is to require the Prosecution to present any evidence they wish that goes beyond the submissions for admission already made by leading Mr. Coo viva voce. We think, subject to any objection that may be taken that it would be in order to introduce through him the provenance report as a short-cut, and on the face of it, also to introduce his February 2007 statement if you have that in mind. It's the report that's the issue here and not these two documents, as I understand the position. And if anyone from the Defence thinks otherwise, they should say so before we start. Having heard the evidence, the Trial Chamber will issue a written decision determining the actual admission or rejection of the various exhibits that the Prosecution now tender finally. And that decision will be issued as soon as possible after the completion of the evidence, but by that I mean very quickly. It will be issued this week; whether it's tomorrow or Friday is the only question. That's what I intended to say, Mr. Hannis. Does that answer your questions or do you have something else to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It answers many of them, Your Honour, but I still do have something to say, if I may, before Mr. Coo comes in. With regard to the reports, they have been put into e-court now and they have exhibit numbers. So for purposes of identification I just wanted to state on the record what those were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you mean the reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The -- Coo's report, part 1, part 2, and the addendum --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These should be removed from e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And they should become part of a submission to the registry in support of the admission of the documents from the bar table, as was suggested -- or at least -- just let me think about this a little more. Since they are submissions in support of the admission of these documents, not strictly from the bar table, nevertheless they are a part of material which should not be in the process here but should be re-filed with the registry as a motion in support of your -- the admission of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I wondered about referring to their numbers, P2858, 59, and 60, parts 1, 2, and the addendum, and having them marked, not admitted, but then they are -- they become the Prosecution's submission for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I understand. The proper course to follow is to have them re-filed as a motion for admission of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. We will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's a written -- essentially, it's a written filing just like that made by Messrs. Ackerman, Fila, and Ivetic now in support of their case resisting submission, and you would make the same document available as a filing in support of the actual admission. And we will confine consideration to the documents that you now seek to have admitted and we will take account also in making our decision of the evidence you lead from Mr. Coo, including the provenance report and the statement of February 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And they can both have exhibit numbers and will be part of the process, the trial process -- the evidence, rather, in the trial for us to consider.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The provenance report does have an exhibit number of 2845 and the witness statement is now 2861.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One thing that doesn't yet have an exhibit number is the Excel spreadsheet that I e-mailed to you and the parties last night which has 193 items listed. These are the ones that we are seeking admission for, reduced from the original provenance report list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, just live me one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That document should be filed along with the report as part of the motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And then for purposes of our discussion today, I should tell Your Honours and the parties that I went through that list of 193 this morning and I identified I think five that we will drop from the list, and I can announce that now so that we don't have any further discussion about them. Number 3 is P986, a constitution. We're not going to pursue that because there's a version of the constitution already in as part of the agreed facts under P856. Item number 9 on the list Criminal Code of the Republic of Serbia, that was previously admitted as an exhibit -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, I have a list of numbers on mine but yours don't. I'll just read the exhibit number. Exhibit Number 1023, we're no longer seeking to admit; 1031 and 1064 was on the list but that was admitted I think by your decision yesterday, according to my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think I must have been saying it had already been admitted yesterday. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Maybe that's -- maybe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think anything was admitted yesterday. I think it was simply confirmed that two items had already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was it yesterday Your Honour announced the decision on bar table submission number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, I see, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're referring to a different process. Yes. Okay. And the final one?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's it, Your Honour, I believe. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've only got four: 986, 1023, 1031, 1064.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 1020 as well, Your Honour. That was previously admitted on the 10th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I think one item I overlooked, there is attached to the notification of Mr. Coo's evidence another list of exhibits to be tendered which is in addition to I think the main list. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think all of those now are covered. Either they've already been admitted or they are ones that are attached as an appendix to his witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In fact, the only ones that matter are VJ General Staff collegium minutes, because the first three are the report and the fourth one is the provenance report and the fifth one is the statement of the 27th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But if you go beyond past the VJ collegium minutes, there are some other minutes beginning with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- 2801, but those are attached to his statement, and we will be seeking to tender those as well. I indicated that in the e-mail that we sent last night I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. But these are then additional to the list of 190 or so minus five that you've now given us?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, these are in addition to the 188 now remaining on this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. So is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour. I had proposed putting his provenance report in, his witness statement pursuant to 92 ter, but I can lead him live about that if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no. The provenance report, I'm suggesting to you would be admissible 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I saw shake -- nodding heads from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the statement itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Likewise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what I propose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's perfectly acceptable. So we can now have Mr. Coo -- sorry, no. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, very briefly. The Coo 65 ter document and your ruling, there is some tension between the two of them and I'm satisfied that Your Honour has noticed that and that his testimony will be in accordance with your ruling today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. We followed --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But there is tension there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We followed your invitation yesterday to treat it as a motion, conscious of the possibility that there is tension between looking at material for one purpose and being sure that you exclude it from your mind for another purpose, but we thought that your suggestion was an admirable way of making clear the distinction --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- and removing the point of confusion that would otherwise have existed, and everyone seemed to accept that was appropriate. Mr. Hannis didn't, I acknowledge, because he still considered that the report was a better way of doing it -- of presenting the evidence, but I'm -- I was hoping that this was a very transparent way of ensuring that the evidence was confined to the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No question about that and I think I've probably been misunderstood again, which seems to happen to me a lot; it's probably my advanced age. But in any event, Your Honour, the 65 ter filing that says -- the Prosecution tells you what they're going to elicit from Coo tends to be in conflict with your ruling and I don't want to make a big argument about that at this point. I just wanted to point out that I had noticed that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But what do you mean by -- what is the conflict you've identified if it's not what I've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There's a 65 ter filing where they give a summary of what it is they are going to elicit from Coo, and they say that he will describe the organisation, operations, and conduct of the forces of the FRY and Serbia that were active in Kosovo during the time-period relevant to the indictment, will demonstrate the widespread and systematic nature of their operations, detail the structure and function of the VJ and MUP forces present in Kosovo, the command and control of the VJ forces in Kosovo, the unity of command, uninterrupted chain of command and functioning system of discipline --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But if you are successful in keeping out things that it is said a witness is going to speak about, then the success of your opposition will be reflected in the restricted nature of his evidence. Inevitably the 65 ter will then be out of line with it, but as soon as I leave court after having heard his evidence, this goes in the shredder.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I understand that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not part of my thought process when it comes to looking at the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to sit down, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for taking the floor. At this point I would kindly seek an explanation as far as I understood. By your decision, the statement by witness Philip Coo has been entered into evidence as 2861. I would like to say that there is an addendum to this statement which I can't see in the e-court, but in its essence the addendum is something that we have discussed on many occasions. It seems to me that pages from 5 through 10 of the statement actually is the report and not what was your idea when you decided to admit his statement for other reasons, and this is what I wanted to draw attention to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What I'm referring to as his statement is a document which is only four pages followed by an appendix; it's not the addendum to the report. And the decision we've made did not admit the report; it invited Mr. Hannis to withdraw the report in its two parts and the addendum from e-court and re-file all three as part of his motion in support of admission of these various documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is exactly the explanation that I was seeking. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please bring Mr. Coo in now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Coo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We -- it won't surprise you to know we had a few continuing administrative issues to sort out in relation to your evidence. I think we're now ready to hear it, so could you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Hannis will be the first to examine you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Coo. I know you've testified in this building before, and because we both speak English will you try and help me remember to leave a pause between my questions and your answers and vice versa for the sake of the interpreters and the court reporter.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us your name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: It's Philip Coo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how are you currently employed?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I'm employed by the Office of the Prosecutor as the head of the military analysis team.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How long have you worked for the OTP?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: For almost eight years now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you started, what was your position?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I began as an intelligence analyst in the same section.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did you get promoted to your current position?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I became the acting head of the section in August 2004, and act -- and the head of the section in January 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And prior to joining the OTP, can you tell us what your work experience was and in particular any military service.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Before joining the OTP, I was an intelligence officer in the Canadian Army for ten years and had a variety of appointments during that ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in connection with your evidence for this case I want to refer you to two documents. The first one is a provenance report that you prepared. It's dated the 14th of February, 2007. Have you had a chance to look at that before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And are you satisfied that the information contained in that document is true and accurate to the best of your information and belief?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you attest to the Court today that that is your evidence and you would give the same answers if you were asked questions about it today?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Also, did you prepare a document entitled "Witness Statement of OTP Military Analyst Philip Coo" dated the 27th of February of this year?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Likewise, did you have a chance to review it before coming to court?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And same question: Are you satisfied it's true and accurate, it amounts to your declaration, your evidence in this case, and you would give the same answers if you were asked questions about its contents?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With that, Your Honour, we would tender those two items. The provenance report is Exhibit P2845, the witness statement is Exhibit P2861, pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, in the course of your work in connection with this case, we all know that you prepared a report that had two parts and an addendum, which now is going to be treated as the Prosecution's submission to admit exhibits selected therefrom and related thereto. I want to ask you in general about the document-collection process related to this Kosovo case. First of all, can you tell me when OTP began collecting documents relating to the Kosovo conflict.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: To my knowledge, the collecting began immediately upon the entry of KFOR into Kosovo after the end of the period of NATO bombing in June 1999. I had joined the OTP in -- at the end of May 1999, and presumably they had done some collecting prior to that but not that I was involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And who was involved in that process beginning in June of 1999?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: A large number of people within the OTP, investigators, lawyers, and analysts. I was involved in some of the missions to collect documents in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned missions, so how was that collection process done, physically speaking?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Once the Serb forces had withdrawn from Kosovo, the members of the OTP followed KFOR in there and visited a variety of sites looking for documents. The sites included VJ facilities, MUP facilities, and municipal offices and a variety of other official buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where did it take place? You say "Kosovo." Was it limited to one area of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: It was all over Kosovo, to my awareness. I can't say that it included every municipality, but as far as I know, they covered most of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in broad terms, what kinds of evidence or documents were collected in that process?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: We collected a number of VJ documents, documents belonging to the Military Territorial Organisation from the Pristina Military District, MUP documents from MUP buildings, documents from the temporary Executive Council, a civilian body in Kosovo; and a miscellany of other types of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition to proactively going out and collecting documents, did the OTP investigators involved in this process also have materials given to them?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Some investigators did in -- during the conduct of their investigations were given documents. I think this was a relatively small number, and I'm not aware of the details. Some of the details are evident in the way that the evidence is registered in our evidence unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And over approximately what time period did this physical evidence-collection process in Kosovo extend from June 1999?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The -- the bulk of it occurred in the summer of 1999, in July -- late June, July, and August, and missions continued through the rest of 1999 and into 2000, by which time the number of buildings or locations to exploit was declining.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So in addition and subsequent to this process, what other methods were employed to try and obtain documentation about that conflict?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: We drafted requests for assistance to various states, but in particular to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and its successor states asking for specific categories of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is an acronym that we used a lot during the course of this trial, RFA, does that stand for request for assistance?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges a little bit about how that process works in general terms.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The -- the investigation team or trial team associated with a particular case identifies the types of information it thinks that it needs and drafts an official request sent to the state on behalf of the Prosecutor requesting that they provide the information or the documents in question. In some cases we have to try to figure out what types of documents they would have -- not in every case did we know the specific types of documents, so in some cases the requests were relatively broad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know how the process works once the request is drafted and sent out from the OTP? Do you know where it goes and how it's handled?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Once it's drafted, I believe it goes to the -- through the embassy in The Hague to the -- to Belgrade. This is in particular to requests going to the former Yugoslavia or Serbia. The request goes to Belgrade, where they send it to the appropriate organisation and if they have the document or the information requested, hopefully -- and they have provided those documents in the forms of official responses, which work their way back through the same pathway back to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a body called the commission for cooperation with The Hague in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I have heard of that body, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know of the nature of its involvement in this process?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I believe it's a coordinating body, through which our requests for assistance and their responses pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition to trying to obtain materials pursuant to the RFA process, have you or other members of the investigating team from the OTP engaged in missions to archives in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: We -- we have. We managed to get archive access in -- arranged in late March 2006 to the archives in Serbia. These included the MUP and the VJ. That archive access was actually followed up by mission to the VJ and the MUP archives in May and June 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Had there been attempts prior to 2006 to try and get physical access to those archives?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: There had been a number of attempts, and a number of times we put in RFAs that we could facilitate the provision of material if they would allow us access to archives because sometimes the responses to requests for assistance were that our requests were overly broad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you participate in any of these archive missions yourself?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I participated in the first archive mission in June -- late May/June 2006 and a second archive mission in August 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And to where did you go on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: On the first mission we went to the MUP archive, although I hesitate to call it an archive. It was a -- we were shown to a collection of documents that we had been told had been compiled expressly for the purpose of consolidating all documentation that the MUP had in connection to Kosovo in 1998/1999, and the MUP told us that the collection was called the dossier KiM or dossier Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you say you hesitate to use the term "archive." Why is that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: This wasn't the archive for all of the Ministry of the Interior in Serbia. It was a collection, and we had been told by the person heading the archive at that time -- correction, by the person responsible for the dossier KiM that the collection had been put together on the order of General Sreten Lukic in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was the person who told you that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, it was a Colonel Milan Petrovic, who is a MUP officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you give the Court a general description of what this collection consisted of.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: It's in a -- the collection, Your Honours, is in a relatively small room. At a rough guess it's probably 20 square metres. The documentation is arranged in ceiling-height cupboards around the perimeters of the room. They have an electronic log of the documents. We were allowed to peruse the log and the documents themselves. They had a staff of I think about five people managing the collection, and it's located in the Serbian Ministry of the Interior building in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the information you were told was that this was the complete collection of MUP documents concerning Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: We were told that that was the idea behind the collection. There was some missing -- in our view, some missing documents were documents that we would have expected to have seen in there which weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was missing that you would have expected to have been in that collection.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: We were expecting to see references or documentation covering, for example, operations by the special police units or PJP. We were expecting also to see daily reports produced by the MUP staff in Kosovo. We already had a few of those that we'd collected in Kosovo in 1999 and were looking for the remained of them, but we didn't find those when we reviewed the registry -- the dossier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you inquire of the personnel that you were dealing with there about the absence of those particular types of documents?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: We did, and we were told, not specific to these documents, but generally in regard to missing documents that it was possible that some documentation remained in the Secretariats of the Interior, or SUPs, which had been moved out of Kosovo and into parts of southern Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Subsequent to that time, did you make any attempts to try and locate those type of documents in the SUPs or obtain them from the SUPs through RFAs?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: We did a follow-up mission in August, primarily to review more MUP documentation and this mission was to address these -- to address the fact that we didn't believe that the dossier KiM was -- represented all the Kosovo-related documents. We asked to be shown any other -- or be allowed to review documentation in any other departments of the MUP, and on that mission in August 19 -- August 2006, we were taken around various departments within the MUP in Belgrade where we were shown a very small number of remaining documents pertaining to 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you on this mission locate any of those types of documents that you had expected to find in the collection?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: We didn't find anything along the lines of the daily reports of the MUP staff or any documentation connected to PJP operations. What we found were primarily administrative-type reports and a very small number. These weren't -- these weren't archives of the departments that we were shown to. We were generally shown binders -- a small number of binders or folders containing documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, subsequent to that did you make any inquiries about the existence of such documents and where they might be?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: It hasn't been pursued to my knowledge further than that because we were told that we'd been provided everything that they have and shown everything that they have in relation to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean there have been no RFAs since March 2006?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were RFAs, Your Honour, but not, to my knowledge, since August 2006, save for a couple of very specific ones but not connected to these MUP documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in that answer you're referring to RFAs regarding MUP documents. There have been other RFAs?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: There have been. There was one RFA connected to MUP documents after August 2006, but that was -- that was merely part of the process we have to go through for requesting documents, which is when we see something in an archive or in a MUP office that we'd like, we then have to come back here and draft an RFA requesting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't recall, Mr. Coo, if you were aware or had seen any pleadings that had been filed in this case by the Lukic Defence concerning their efforts to obtain documents from the MUP.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I have a vague recollection of one, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether that one indicated that they had received any materials that you had previously sought and not been able to obtain?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the VJ, did you partake in an archive mission to the VJ in 2006?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: We did in part of the same mission in May/June 2006. After we'd finished reviewing the dossier KiM in the MUP building, we went to the VJ Military History Institute archive in Belgrade. This was located in a temporary location, in the basement of the military high school after its previous location -- because its previous location had been bombed during the NATO bombing period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: This resembled what we expected of an archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could you explain what you mean by that answer. In what way was it different than what you described about the MUP?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: It had the contemporaneous registers of archive holdings, and it had the -- it was the complete collection or seemed to be the complete collection of all VJ and JNA documentation, we were told, since 1945, but we were interested in 1998/1999 and it seemed to have what we were looking for, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I want to, before I move on to some questions about other types of information -- or other sources of documents that are on the list of documents that the Prosecution is proposing to tender, I want to ask you about your witness statement. There is an appendix attached to that including a number of documents that are now marked as Exhibits 2801 through 2813 as well as some other items that had already been tendered or had numbers. That regards VJ collegium minutes. These documents are documents that were most recently received?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. The VJ collegium minutes were received I think in late 2005/2006 in response to an RFA. It took a while to get these translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the heading to that appendix you indicate that the items on this list in the appendix that start with the ERN of K053 were ones that were selected from your archives missions in the summer of 2006?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct, and they took until the end of October 2006 to be handed over to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, these don't appear on the annex that I have to the statement, but they do appear on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think at the time his statement was prepared on the -- was it the 27th of February? - they had not yet received an exhibit number. I can advise the Court now on the record what those exhibit numbers are or provide another document. What I propose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've just given them, but the ones I have on that list all have exhibit numbers in the 900s.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The ones that do have numbers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, none of them don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that -- I may be looking at a different --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's an administrative matter, but it's to ensure that nothing is omitted here by oversight.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can I ask Your Honour what the first document you have on the list is. Is it a war diary?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Does it have an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It doesn't, but all the VJ collegium documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- minutes do have exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I thought that's what your question was confined to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I am referring to the ones that an ERN of K053 which start from the third item on the list were items that were recovered during the archive mission. Do you see the third item, the MUP staff meeting of 16 February 1999 has a ERN of K053-4095.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I was referring to those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give me a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But what I propose to do, Your Honour, is attach the appendix to my list of what is now 188 items and include it with the submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've misunderstood your question now that I re-read it. You are saying the collegium minutes do have numbers and the others don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No problem. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your appendix, Mr. Coo, you do list some remarks about the relevancy of those items and you explain the provenance, so I'll ask you nothing more about that now. With regard to your provenance report, there were originally, I think, 400-some items on that list. We've now reduced it to 188. And the last column in that report is entitled: "MAT comments" what does MAT stand for?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's the military analysis team.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And these are your comments about where these documents came from and comments about the authenticity. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: They appear to break down into five or six general categories, and let me ask you about that. You do describe this in your provenance report. A number of them are received pursuant to RFAs; correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There are a few official documents such as gazettes or decrees. There are a number of items listed as being acquired during the document exploitation mission to Kosovo. Is that the first thing you were telling us about how these documents were collected?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And then there are some unofficial or public sources, such as media reports, newspaper items, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have I -- and you also mention web sites. Let me ask you about the web sites. The two that I recall you obtained documents from are what you described as the official VJ web site and the official MUP site. Can you explain to the Court a little bit about that. How did you find the official VJ web site, when did that happen, and what information do you have to give the Court some assurance that it is what it purported to be?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I don't recall, Your Honours, how I first became aware of the web sites, but I felt that they were the official web sites or I had no reason to believe otherwise because the information on them appeared to be corroborated by other documentation that we had. It was relatively innocuous for the most part. References to, for example, the mandate of the VJ derived from the constitution, diagrams of the rank system, and another link to press releases.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was this web site in English?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: It had both English and VJ -- sorry, B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you downloaded those items that are on your list of documents that were used in connection with preparation of your reports?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct. I saved electronic copies and printed off hard copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You may have stated this in your answer, but did the information -- the contents conform with other information you had from VJ documents or from VJ witnesses that you may have interviewed?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, if we look at the web site -- these web sites today, are they in any different form, generally speaking, from the form in which you initially discovered them and have subsequently looked at them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, they've changed. They're now the Army of Serbia. I looked yesterday and it's the Army of Serbia web site. I couldn't find -- and I asked a B/C/S speaker to see if they could find any archived information from the time I checked, and they couldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And so far as the MUP archive is concerned, is it any different from what it was before -- the MUP web site?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same goes for the MUP web site, too, Your Honour, it's now slightly different. I didn't check it yesterday. I had checked it a few times after I downloaded the information, and at those times it still contained the same information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think these addresses ended ".yu." Has that changed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I typed in "VJ" I think, Your Honour, it was vj.yu yesterday. It remained vj.yu but automatically directed me to the new Army of Serbia web site, but I can't be certain about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with connection to the MUP web site, the documents you downloaded from there, did the content likewise show itself to be consistent with other information you had from other MUP documents or interviews of MUP witnesses?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there anything to indicate to you that the information obtained from the web site was incorrect?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Not the information I reviewed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And again, the nature of the documents from the web sites that you have included in your report, what types of matters does that relate to? Is that information about any operations that were conducted, for example?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: They did have, from my recollection, some references to operations. I don't believe I downloaded that information. The type of information I downloaded were references to the mandate of the VJ, the descriptions of its structure, and the roles of different types of units and one or two press releases or press statements. And with the MUP web site, I downloaded similar information but also including references to the -- the information they had on the number of MUP killed or wounded in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, one other general area of documents or provenance for documents on your list are several that are identified as having been received by the Prosecutor, Mrs. Del Ponte, from either Zoran Djindjic or General Pavkovic in July 2002. What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I wasn't involved directly in this but was told around the time that -- by the investigation team leader dealing with Kosovo at that time that General Pavkovic had given a collection of documents to the Prosecutor on a visit that she had to Belgrade in 2002. Prime Minister Djindjic was handed part of this package by General Pavkovic, according to the written note taken at the time by the Prosecutor's political advisor. The other package, I believe, according to the note was handed later the same day directly by General Pavkovic to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you've reviewed most or all of those documents that were received on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in terms of the -- their appearance and regularity, do you have any comment you can make to the Court about that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: As far as I can tell, they looked like official VJ documents, primarily operational reports, such as orders issued in 1998 and 1999. Also included in the package was a large document known as the -- the war diary of the 3rd Army forward command post. And finally I think the -- the only other document falling outside the VJ operational reports category was the minutes of the Joint Command covering July to October 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Had General Pavkovic been indicted by then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe he had. He had just finished as Chief of the General Staff at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to ask you about some of the RFAs. I think there are four or five different RFA numbers in the list of documents in your provenance report. One number that appears quite often is 0119 and in some places it has a letter after it such as E or F and sometimes there's a reference to VJ combat reports. Can you tell the Court what that request for assistance was and to whom it was addressed?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was the -- essentially the original request to Yugoslavia and its successor states aimed at getting VJ documentation. There were a series of refinements to the original RFA 119, hence the lettering from A to F I think, and these refinements reflected both an increase in our knowledge about the types of documentation that the VJ was producing, but also the refinements were connected to 54 bis proceedings in the Milosevic case and the -- the assertions from Yugoslavia or Serbia that our requests were too broad. So in response to this, we attempted to refine the requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Another one is 0174. Do you recall what that's for? At least a couple of them make a reference to Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That RFA dealt specifically with documentation of the Joint Command which we were seeking in, I believe -- or since 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, while we're talking about that, can you tell us what your experience was in trying to obtain Joint Command documents. Did you have any difficulty in that process?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: It was quite a torturous process. We first requested the documentation in 2002. The response, I believe, to that request was that the Joint Command ceased to exist after October 1998 and the documentation had been destroyed by NATO bombing. We subsequently came across -- we had additional information to believe that this wasn't the case because we -- we believed that NATO bombing wouldn't have destroyed Joint Command documentation being produced during the NATO bombing period itself, because those documents wouldn't have been handed in to the archive, which had allegedly been bombed in Belgrade. So we continued pushing for a better response. At some point we -- we were provided with a 17 April 1999 General Staff suggestion directed at the 3rd Army. That suggestion cited a Joint Command order of the 15th of April, 1999. I believe we requested that 15 April Joint Command order specifically and with no success. We then inserted the reference to this Joint Command order into a bigger request for I think about 75 or so VJ documents, and the response to that request included the 15 April Joint Command order. We then proceeded to use this 15 April Joint Command order as evidence that the documentation had not been destroyed by NATO bombing and continued to press through 54 bis proceedings in Milosevic and through RFAs for the provision of Joint Command documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would indicate that the 17 April 1999 suggestion from the General Staff is Exhibit P1487, already in evidence, and I don't have a reference to the 15 April Joint Command order but I believe that is also in evidence already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I need to check that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: A couple of other RFA numbers, if you can tell us, 309. There are a number of documents that appear on the list related -- or identified as responses to that one.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I don't recall what the subject was. I -- it might have been MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, a number of them do appear to make reference to MUP. Another number is 1016 and there's a reference to VJ brigade reports.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I think 1016 was drafted in response to documentation that was provided in the Defence phase of Milosevic through Defence witnesses, but I'm not positive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: A higher number would indicate that that was later in time?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, the remaining category or body of documents are ones that are listed as having been either received by an investigator from the OTP - I think there are a handful of those with no further information - and the ones as listed as having been recovered during the document exploitation mission and -- or acquired during a post-war OTP document exploitation mission to Kosovo, oftentimes with no further details. Can you tell the Judges any other general considerations you took into account in connection with those documents to satisfy yourself about their reliability and suitability to be included in your initial report.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I looked for official stamps, signatures, indications that an official format was being followed. I also looked at the contents of the documents and, as often as possible, tried to group documents with similar information or corroborating information together in my report. And generally, these were acquired independently of one another. I couldn't see any -- in any of the documents acquired in the -- through these two means from witnesses -- correction -- from individuals handing them to investigators or from members of the OTP collecting documents from various facilities in Kosovo. I couldn't see any indication that -- to suggest that these were forged or had been tampered with. For the most part, the information in these documents was quite -- quite mundane or innocuous and didn't strike me as the type of information that anyone intent on misleading us would bother forging.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are there any being tendered that you harbour some doubt about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't think of any, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And does that go for as well -- I think there are about two or three as -- listed as having been received or obtained at the UCK headquarters, perhaps received from somebody from the KLA. Does that fact alone give you cause for concern about the authenticity of those documents?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: It would give me normally cause for concern, but I believe -- I can't remember exactly what documents those were. I don't believe that those were the documents that had the information of a kind that would be forged or intended to mislead. The only document I'm aware of that anyone thought might be a forgery was a list with, I believe, an introductory sentence saying: Names of Albanians to be liquidated, and as far as I'm aware that wasn't used -- that definitely wasn't used by me and hasn't been an exhibit in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can confirm to the Court that document has not been presented in our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. And did you also look at these documents based on your knowledge or experience of other known VJ and MUP and political documents with an eye to the form and style of how they were prepared?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I did. A lot of these -- although a lot of these documents were incorporated into my original Milosevic report before we had the number of documents that we do from, for example, the VJ archive, nonetheless I think the -- the format of most of these documents corresponded to the type of format you would expect of, for example, a military order or a military daily combat report. They had the types of subheadings that I would expect that I've seen in the Canadian Army's and other armies' combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with the passage of time which -- I take it you've had a chance to look at hundreds or thousands of additional documents that the provenance is well-known. Is there anything to indicate that those documents discovered in the document exploitation mission are not authentic because they're different in form or style?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Nothing to my knowledge, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One other general area that there are a handful of documents, a few that were presented as Defence exhibits in the Milosevic case. I think most of them on our list are ones that were brought in by then-General Delic. Are you satisfied as to the authenticity of those?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The ones that I've used -- that I did use in my report, as far as I can tell, appear to be authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: There are hundreds of others that I haven't really reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no more questions for Mr. Coo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can we have a very short break to discuss -- in fact, it may help us reduce our questions down to a minimum?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, we can break now and begin again at quarter to, I think, if that's convenient. Mr. Coo, the usher will escort you from the court and show you where you should wait while we have the break. [The witness stands down].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume at 10.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will follow the indictment, and I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Same here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the saga has ended, Mr. Coo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your evidence is complete; thank you for coming to give it. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have another proposal or submission. I have already agreed about that with Mr. Hannis, but we waited until the last moment for some translations; however, the CLSS let us down. Still, we would like to tender three records of senior staff meetings of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. Those are 3D557, 3D558, and 3D559. Those are senior staff meetings of the 3rd December 1998, 6th January 1999, and 28th January 1999. The first exhibit, 3D557, a senior staff meeting of the 3rd December, has been translated and it's in the system. The second exhibit, 3D558, the senior staff meeting of the 6th of January, we only have the original in B/C/S and we are expecting a translation from the CLSS. And the third exhibit, 3D559, the senior staff meeting of the 28th of January, has an original in B/C/S in the system and we are expecting the translation, the deadline was yesterday, and we hope we will get it today. We believe that the CLSS is also snowed under, but we hope that we will get the translations of these two exhibits before the end of this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis, your position on these?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had discussed that with Mr. Visnjic. We have no objections. A number of these are already in. As we indicated, Your Honours, finding the most relevant bits sometimes is not always easy, but I think, often times oftentimes it's necessary to read the whole meeting to get a sense of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The effect of introducing these, though, at this stage with your consent is that they form part of the picture we'll be looking at in 98 bis? You accept that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, we'll admit the first one, 3D557, and the other two will be marked for identification pending translation. You should file a note, Mr. Visnjic, when translated. Mr. Hannis, I should have asked you to clarify the position with these exhibit numbers of the documents attached to Mr. Coo's statement. I know you gave us a list of 2803, I think, to 2813, but can we be clear where they start.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I intended to do was attach that list of those that we wished to tender along with the list of 188.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's going to be a supplement to the report; in other words, a qualification of the report when it's filed as a -- as part of the motion for admission of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, I was just going to identify it as a separate list and identify it as having come from the appendix to Witness Coo's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But if the 2803 is the third item there the report written by MUP staff member Pesic, if that's the case, does that mean that the first two don't have exhibit numbers, two war diaries, or do they have numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: They do have numbers, Your Honour. The first -- the first seven items on the list will be 2801 through 2807, then there is Exhibit P2591 already admitted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after 2591 we would resume with 2808 consecutively through 2813.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Which would then take Your Honour I hope to P941.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Which is already in evidence on the 22nd of January. P939 that was already admitted, as well as 938, 935. The following page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So -- but hold on again. 941 you say has already been admitted, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Umm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It doesn't say so in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Did I say 941? I have a note that it was admitted on the 22nd of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm having -- yes, that's what it indicates in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've also tried to go through them. It's also one of the senior staff meetings. I have it noted that 5941 [as interpreted] should have been admitted through Philip Coo, not through an earlier decision. I'm sorry. For the record, P-941.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will check when we are reviewing it. You then say that the next few have been admitted, that's down to 935. 933 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, on page A-5 at the top, 933 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm on A-4 at the moment but -- but 939, 938, and 935 bear to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what my notes indicate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's one that we will include on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Stop there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They have all been admitted and then 25 and 22 have yet to be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what is the next surprise you have in store for us, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I looked outside before I came in. I did not -- I see Mr. O'Sullivan. He's going to let my surprise out.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. One small matter to advise the Chamber that yet the Milutinovic Defence and Mr. Hannis met and we anticipate filing a further joint submission on stipulations which may come tomorrow, we expect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In -- is that stipulated by everyone?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'd have to check on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we're still on administrative things, there's one other matter I wanted to bring to the Court's attention relating to some documents we had just received yesterday from the Office of the Prosecutor -- excuse me. The day before yesterday, these documents came. We filed a notice for judicial notice and I don't know if that's made it into the system yet. This relates to information -- official investigative information received --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have seen this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just wanted to make sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We do have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I don't know whether the Prosecution needs to respond. I just want to make sure that they were aware of it and they asked for time, if they needed, to relating to Mr. Protic's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would be very helpful, Mr. Hannis, to have an instant response to that. I don't mean this minute, but if it was possible -- I'll give you a -- well, if it was possible to respond by tomorrow morning, it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll try and do that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand it may not be. I'm not making an order to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll try and do that, Your Honour. I would indicate to you I anticipate that we will object to the request that you take judicial notice of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. All right. Thank you. And Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm a bit lost but I would like the Prosecution to assist me if they may. Are the following numbers tendered: 936, 930, 934, and 937? Have they been tendered or admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Give me the numbers again, Mr. Visnjic, sorry. Just take them slowly. The first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first number is 936.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't see it among the list here, nor is 930 there, nor is 934, nor 937. They don't appear to be tendered at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, we have not tendered them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, Your Honour, we would like to tender these exhibits --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's a matter --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- just once again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a matter you should deal directly with Mr. Hannis on, and if you reach agreement, you should tender them with a very brief written filing and do it today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That -- and they will only be admitted if it's by agreement of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk wants to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Just as a final precaution, Your Honour, we would just like to keep the record open as a follow-up to what Mr. Visnjic just did. There may be just a few exhibits, a handful, and there may not be, but just want to make absolutely certain that all the exhibits that should be tendered are, and if we could have till the end of the day on that or at least till -- part of the day, we would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the filing that you tender can deal with those and any others that you can persuade Mr. Hannis to agree to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis, where do we go from here?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, out into the sunshine for an hour, I hope. No, Your Honour, we -- I did want to bring a couple of matters to your attention. There was an additional witness -- well, there were three additional witnesses that we had hoped to present to you but we have not been able to. One of them was Mr. Lilic. Mr. Stamp was going to file something with you tomorrow indicating the status regarding our efforts to do that for informational purposes and whatever action we might seek to take in the future or request of the Court. Just wanted to bring that to your attention. We had also hoped to have Mr. Byrnes and General Clark here. Your ruling allowed it to be possible for Mr. Byrnes to come, but because of urgent personal matters we were not able to get him here before the close of our evidence. And General Clark, as you know, our filing on the appeal is due today, so we'll be filing something on that, and if it's appropriate we'll file something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. We thought it was due yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I know, I've seen the draft this morning, Your Honour, so I know it did not get filed yesterday but we will advise the Court of that. And with the same you allowance that Mr. Sepenuk requested to check the status of all the exhibits that we think are in and be sure that they are in, at this time, Your Honour, we would rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, well, "rest" not in the formal sense, I take it, because there's nothing we can do until -- if there is an appeal in Clark and if the Appeals Chamber are prepared to take the view that it's in time, then there's nothing that we can do until that has been resolved. I mean, that effectively stymies the 98 bis process.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't secure about how the Court would proceed in light of that matter pending, whether we would go forward with the 98 bis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, how can we? We would be delighted to if you can demonstrate to us how it can be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought that perhaps you would proceed that way, and if the ruling came out a certain way, the Prosecution would make an application to re-open its case and present General Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see. I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What happens if someone has been acquitted by then?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that's the Prosecution's loss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But in terms of the Defence presentation of 98 bis, I hope that I would not be presenting General Clark or Mr. Byrnes as witnesses who would subtract from the Prosecution's evidence. So the fact that they came after the 98 bis wouldn't result in any unfairness to the Defence in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, on the question of whether it's possible to proceed with a 98 bis hearing with an outstanding appeal that would lead to a further witness being led.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, this is certainly a matter that I think should be discussed among my colleagues, because as you pointed out, this does lead to a potential problem, and one that requires more thought than I can give it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It probably is to the Defence advantage; on the other hand, the test for re-opening the case at first blush couldn't be met by succeeding in an appeal when you already have in mind the calling of the witness. I thought the re-opening test was that you couldn't foresee leading that witness at the time of the trial. So I wonder -- I mean, have you thought this through completely, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I have not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, in that case, this will require to be discussed later. Now, we are going to sit tomorrow, whatever happens. It may only be briefly, just to deal with anything outstanding that we can deal with, but if there are to be submissions made on this, perhaps they should be in the third session later or -- is that long enough for you to think about it or do you want to make these submissions tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Perhaps tomorrow morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If it was easy to have the 98 bis hearing, you would be pushing at an open door; but I was surprised, I have to say, that that was thought to be feasible. Anyone have any other matter to raise at this stage? We will sit then at 9.00 tomorrow. I don't expect we'll be in court for much of tomorrow, but you may have to be available depending on what we try to determine in the course of tomorrow. For example, we may need to give thought to this question, and rather than leave it hanging I think we would want to make a decision if we could so that further procedure is clear, including possibly the date at -- on which the Defence case will begin. So we'll adjourn now and resume at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 22nd day of March, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.09 a.m.,
